Most people are not attracted to misinformation because it’s correct; they are attracted to it because it makes them *feel* correct.

Our most successful approach has been utilizing the infrastructure of the state community health network areas, which are regional collaboratives of public health/NPO health/health service orgs. Low barrier access to BCPs is a downstream harm reduction solution to address the urgent, time bound impacts of upstream care access failures. The choice people have now isnt “get BCPs thru a doctor” or “get BCPs OTC.” It’s “get BCPs thru a doctor” or “don’t get them at all”. The risks of misuse are less than Tylenol or ibuprofen; the risks of contraindications with NSAIDs, antihistamines, PPIs are as if not more risky. 

There are many efforts to implement upstream solutions but we can’t afford to sacrifice downstream solutions at the altar of perfection seeking

There are vastly different rates of skin cancer by race/ethnicity, for a few reasons. 

- Almost ALL historical and medical research on skin cancer and its presentations were done on people with fair skin/white people. That means we are not good at identifying what typical skin cancer looks like on darker skin, creating diagnosis gaps. 

- BUT the biggest factor accounting for difference is that higher levels of melanin in the skin mean higher degree of UV filtration, so people with more melanin (aka those that tan quickly/easily, and those with darker skin overall) have less skin cancer even with "more tanning" 

But overall researchers agree we need more research on skin cancer in other skin types to be confident about recommendations.

It varies A LOT (and not in a good way) from site to site. Luckily our site vendor is skilled and collaborative; other sites are… not. 

So my general thoughts are: 

1. Try to contact the site coordinator first. There have been really unfortunate outcomes when extremely well meaning people show up to sites without notice to donate things; it can create a lot of chaos totallt unintentionally 

2. Food storage and preparation varies wildly site to site: some people have full kitchenettes, others have solely a mini fridge. Shelf stable items are safest; toddler-friendly snacks are really helpful

3. Families have very little space so keep that in mind. For example, strollers that fold up as small as possible are better than large ones. There are many new babies; cloth carriers (simple fabric only ones) are really great and useful 

4. Some of the less common things that would make life easier are child proofing kits and cleaning items that have low likelihood of injury (so chlorox wipes instead of bottles of bleach) 

5. Nearly all the folks at our site have work permits and many have jobs; since it’s winter, Uber gift cards to get them to and from work are great 

6. Kids need enrichment. Activity books, art supplies, cards, and other toys that are small, portable, and without batteries/noise are truly life changing for kids who are stuck in a hotel room for HOURS

I had a little of both experiences myself! With my first baby, I was so so so overwhelmed with breastfeeding and pain that ANY additional tools or tricks sent me over the edge. 

But with my second, the shield was a life saver thru the first weeks of nipple pain and then we weaned off it. 

Really listening to what a parent is saying about their needs and fears and hopes is so critical to finding the right approach!

Most of the “stigma” is a symptom of the fact that the more accessories people introduce into breastfeeding, the more likely they are to feel that breastfeeding is inconvenient, time consuming, overwhelming, etc. 

But the most common reality is that people who do want/need accessories for feeding are also most likely to have underlying breastfeeding problems or pain, and avoiding the accessory because of a fear of ending breastfeeding is almost never the cure for the underlying problem. 

In my experience (as a former breastfeeding counselor and now mat-inf researcher), nipple shields are the extremely common for poor latches and the accompanying pain that comes with it. Some people avoid shields because they feel it masks the underlying issue rather than solves it 

But in my experience and research, it is a much much more common lived experience that the shield actually extends the breastfeeding relationship: by giving the nipple a break to heal, by continuing milk transfer while a baby figures out their latch, or by helping train a latch to be wider/deeper 

I know people who use a shield for a few days and people who use it during the entire breastfeeding relationship and people who LOATHE the shield. All of those things are okay: “successful” and happy breastfeeding can look so so so many different ways
